entry.title: The first e-ink monitor that doesn't make me want to throw it out the window
entry.summary: After a month with the Dasung Paperlike 13.3, I finally understand who this thing is for.
entry.content:
I have wanted to like e-ink monitors for a decade. The pitch is irresistible: a display that looks like paper, doesn't glow into your eyes at midnight, and sips power. The reality has usually been a ghosting, flickering mess that costs more than a good laptop. So when the newest generation arrived at my door, I braced for disappointment.

Instead, I've spent the last thirty days writing, editing, and even browsing on a screen that refreshes fast enough to feel like a slightly sluggish LCD, and slow enough to remind you that you're looking at pigment instead of light. It isn't perfect. But for the first time, it's good enough that I keep reaching for it.

The good

Text is the star. At 300 pixels per inch, letters have the crisp, ink-on-paper quality that makes long reading sessions comfortable in a way no backlit panel can match. The front light is warm and even, and it turns off entirely when the room is bright enough — which is the whole point.

Ghosting, the bane of every e-ink device, is managed with a clever adaptive refresh. Scroll a document and the panel switches to a fast, dithered mode; stop, and it snaps a clean full refresh half a second later. After a day I stopped noticing it.

The bad

Video is a non-starter, and anything with fine gradients turns into a newspaper halftone. The stand is flimsy. And at $1,299, this remains a specialist tool for writers, coders, and people whose eyes have simply had enough.

Still: if you spend eight hours a day staring at words, this is the first e-ink monitor I'd actually recommend buying. Which, given the history of this category, feels like a small miracle.

entry.title: Apple quietly drops the price of the Vision Pro
entry.content: The headset now starts at $2,499, down from $3,499.
